title: Thermodynamic Phase Diagrams in $λ$-(BETS)$_2$GaBr$_x$Cl$_{4-x}$ under Physical and Chemical Pressure
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to Superconductor Science and Technology
summary: The evolution of electron correlation in the superconducting state of the mixed-crystal series $λ$-(BETS)$_2$GaBr$_x$Cl$_{4-x}$ was investigated by magnetic and transport measurements. Br concentrations evaluated by electron-probe microanalysis agree well with single-crystal X-ray diffraction refinement. Demagnetization-corrected susceptibility and magnetization of crystals with $x_{c(rf)}$ = 0.22, 0.24, 0.42, and 0.63 all show a diamagnetic superconducting transition. The lower critical field $H_{c1}$, determined from the deviation from the Meissner response, shows a dome-like maximum at $x_{c(rf)}$ = 0.24. The upper critical field $H_{c2}$, obtained from the first high-field magnetoresistance measurements in this system, decreases with increasing Br concentration up to $x_{c(rf)}$ = 0.42, establishing the high-field superconducting boundary on the chemical-pressure side. Combining these results with reported transport data under chemical and physical pressure, we propose a pressure-temperature phase diagram for $λ$-(BETS)$_2$GaCl$_4$. Its double-dome-like structure has a local minimum near x = 0, where a quantum-critical point was proposed at P $\approx$ 0.13 GPa, separating a low-pressure regime of superconductivity coexisting with magnetism and an unconventional metallic state from a higher-pressure regime with conventional metallic behavior. A low-temperature resistivity upturn, previously reported only under physical pressure, is also found under chemical pressure, suggesting that spin-density-wave fluctuations may extend continuously across both pressure axes. The phase diagram overlaps with that of $λ$-(STF)$_2$GaCl$_4$ under physical pressure, indicating that chemical substitution, external pressure, and molecular substitution can be unified in a single bandwidth-controlled phase diagram for $λ$-type molecular superconductors.

title: Driving Atomic Spins through Their Substrate Electrons
summary: Coherent control of single spins on surfaces has relied on decoupling them from the substrate with insulating films, which protects the spin but also removes any electronic means of addressing it. Here we show that a local electric potential can drive an adatom spin through the substrate electrons themselves. An exact reciprocity relation fixes the torque, which equals the change of the local electron density when the moment rotates; the drive map is thus a ground-state property that can be measured independently. The relation also implies sharp selection rules, since point-contact spins, spin-$1/2$ and the central transition of half-integer spins remain dark. On a normal metal the hybridization responsible for the drive also destroys coherence, but on a superconductor the drive survives while substrate damping is confined to subgap transitions. For atomically sharp tips we find Rabi frequencies of several MHz at RF amplitudes of tens of mV, with substrate-limited linewidths below $0.1$~MHz, so that strong hybridization, usually the enemy of spin coherence, becomes an asset.

title: Superconducting Fluctuation Driven Quantum Transport in Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+δ}$ Thin Films
comment: The Central Inferences and Figures of the paper have changed significantly compared to v1 of arXiv: 2511.00803
summary: Superconducting fluctuations (SF), arising from Cooper-pair-driven interactions and electron-electron interactions within the transition regime, can dominate the magnetoconductance (MC) of superconducting thin films near their transition temperature. In some systems, this fluctuation-dominated regime is preceded by a narrow window in which quantum interference effects are manifested as weak antilocalization (WAL) or weak localization (WL). Here, we report magnetotransport measurements on thin films of the high-temperature superconductor Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+δ}$ (BSCCO) that establish SF as the dominant mechanism governing MC across the transition regime. In the narrow temperature window well above $T_c$ where SF does not exist, a cusp in MC can be attributed to WAL-like signature well described by the Hikami--Larkin--Nagaoka (HLN) framework. Closer to the transition ($T_{BKT}$), we observe signatures consistent with Berezinskii--Kosterlitz--Thouless (BKT) correlations, underscoring that the dominant physics is set by collective, pairing-driven behavior rather than single-particle quantum interference. Measurements on non-superconducting control samples show no WAL-like features, indicating that the WAL over narrow temperature window, emerges only in conjunction with superconducting fluctuations. Hall measurements further reveal a concomitant sign reversal of the dominant carrier response, pointing to a substantial reorganization of transverse transport coincident with the onset of superconductivity. Together, these observations establish that magnetotransport in BSCCO thin film.

title: Energy- and momentum-resolved Cooper-pair emission from a cuprate superconductor
summary: Superconductivity arises from Cooper pairing, but conventional photoemission probes electrons individually rather than as pairs. Here we report the observation of Cooper-pair emission from an optimally doped cuprate superconductor using two-electron angle-resolved photoemission (2e-ARPES). Below the superconducting transition, we observe a distinct two-electron emission peak at zero pair binding energy and zero pair momentum that disappears in the normal state, revealing the characteristic fingerprint of a Cooper pair. Unexpectedly, the joint energy distribution broadens markedly along the relative-energy axis as temperature decreases, while the total energy width remains nearly unchanged. This anomalous behavior cannot be explained by instrumental resolution, static disorder or thermal broadening, and instead points to scattering processes involving collective excitations of the superconductor. Our results establish 2e-ARPES as a probe of both Cooper-pair emission and the many-body dynamics of the superconducting state.

title: Analytical mean-field model for electrochemical metallization memristors with a nanoporous matrix: application to Ag/anodic alumina/Al
summary: Memristors based on electrochemical metallization with many filaments are usually modeled by microscopic simulations with many parameters or by phenomenological laws whose parameters are hard to relate to physical quantities. We present an analytical mean-field model for a population of Ag filaments confined in the pores of a nanoporous matrix, built on Ohm's law, Faraday's law and a power-based rupture criterion. The filaments have a truncated normal distribution of cross-sections and rupture leaving lognormally distributed gaps whose median grows with the dissipated power. Gap closing shifts the distribution of squared gaps rigidly, and the model therefore admits closed-form expressions for the switching voltage, the read current, the rupture branch and the high-voltage current. We apply it to Ag/nanoporous anodic alumina/Al structures fabricated from industrial-grade aluminum, with a 2.4$μ$m alumina layer, and measured under ambient conditions. The parameters were fitted to the bipolar sweeps, with the gap dispersion taken from the temporal shape of the read after a pulse. They reproduce the bipolar response, including voltage-controlled negative differential resistance, and predict without refitting the unipolar sweeps and the amplitude of the pulse response, where state memory appears. A second sample, with a larger contact deposited chemically, is described by the same model. In vacuum the devices neither switch nor show negative differential resistance, as expected if adsorbed water supplies the counter reaction; the residual high-voltage current follows ionic hopping conduction.

title: Josephson current along the domain walls in Weyl fully compensated ferrimagnet Ti$_2$MnAl
summary: We experimentally investigate Josephson current in planar Nb-Ti$_2$MnAl-Nb proximity devices, which are formed as junctions between superconducting niobium leads and single crystal flakes of the Weyl fully compensated ferrimagnet Ti$_2$MnAl. We demonstrate well developed Josephson effect for 2~$μ$m distance between the niobium contacts on the Ti$_2$MnAl surface. The measured critical current dependence on the magnetic field $I_c(B)$ shows strong anisotropy for two magnetic field orientations in respect to the Nb-Ti$_2$MnAl-Nb junction plane. For the parallel magnetic field, one can see standard Fraunhofer-like $I_c(B)$ suppression pattern. In contrast, $I_c(B)$ is qualitatively different in normal magnetic field, indicating non-trivial distribution of the Josephson current within the junction plane. From this anisotropy, long-range supercurrent and fast aperiodic fluctuations in $I_c(B)$ we conclude that Josephson current is transferred by the chiral surface states, which emerge along the domain walls in topological compensated ferrimagnet Ti$_2$MnAl. The conclusion on the domain walls is supported by magnetization data for small Ti$_2$MnAl flakes.

title: Growth and fabrication of advanced PbTe-Pb quantum devices
summary: We report recent progress in the growth and fabrication of advanced PbTe-Pb Majorana devices for three-terminal correlation experiments. A critical prerequisite for these devices is a continuous Pb film spanning from the PbTe nanowire to the substrate. In previous studies, PbTe nanowires were spatially separated from the substrate mask, making them unable to fulfill this requirement. To address this issue, we have developed a new growth and fabrication approach. Key fabrication steps are introduced between the PbTe growth and Pb deposition. The top facet of the PbTe nanowire is covered with a Te capping layer before breaking the ultra-high vacuum, enabling ex situ processing for subsequent steps. The mask is then removed, followed by the fabrication of shadow walls. After reloading the chip into the growth chamber, the Te protection layer is removed through thermal decomposition, and the Pb film is subsequently deposited. Notably, a pristine PbTe-Pb interface with an in-situ-equivalent quality can be achieved despite the ex-situ processing. Our technique facilitates the develop of advanced PbTe-Pb quantum devices with complex designs, paving the way toward the realization of topological qubits.

title: Coulomb screening of the orbital inverse Faraday effect in finite-size diffusive conductors
summary: We study the effects of Coulomb screening on the second-order dc response in finite-size diffusive conductors. Starting from the Boltzmann equation supplemented by the self-consistent electrostatic field, we develop a kinetic theory of the inverse Faraday effect for a two-dimensional disk driven by a circularly polarized ac electric field. In this formulation, the first-order charge modulation and the induced electric field are coupled through the Coulomb interaction, and the self-consistent first-order solution determines the nonlinear source for the second-order dc circulating current responsible for the induced magnetic moment. The radial problem is solved numerically using an angular-harmonic expansion and the Chebyshev collocation method. It is shown that in the non-self-consistent approximation the frequency dependence of the second-order dc response has a maximum when the diffusion length associated with the radiation frequency becomes comparable to the sample radius. This behavior is found to be strongly modified by self-consistent screening. We demonstrate that Coulomb screening shifts the maximum of the dc response to a higher drive frequency and suppresses the peak amplitude. This behavior is observed consistently for the area-integrated circulating current and the induced magnetic moment. The obtained results clarify the limitations of the non-self-consistent description of the inverse Faraday effect and show that Coulomb self-consistency is crucial for quantitative predictions of optically induced dc magnetization in finite-size diffusive conductors.

title: Strong phonon-coupled trion emission in Janus homobilayer
summary: Janus transition metal dichalcogenides with broken mirror symmetry provide a novel platform for exploring many-body effects mediated by spin-valley-phonon interactions. Strong electron-phonon coupling demands a precise match between a strong effective dipole moment and nanometer-scale charge confinement. Here, we report thermally robust and enhanced trion emission in a symmetric bilayer WSeS with an S/S stacking configuration. The inward-pointing antiparallel built-in electric fields induce a strong electron confinement effect at the interface, driving dominant trion emission at cryogenic temperatures. Furthermore, a massive electron-phonon coupling strength (3.9) resonant with the optical phonon A_1^2 energy (51 meV) contributes to the thermal stability of this trion emission at elevated temperatures. By tailoring the interfacial architecture in Janus WSeS homobilayers, this study overcomes the thermal decoherence limits inherent to traditional semiconductor systems, offering novel insights into room-temperature many-body interactions.

title: Disentangling Spin and Orbital Contributions in the Search for Altermagnetic Terahertz Conversion in RuO2
summary: Rutile RuO2 has emerged as a prominent candidate altermagnet, yet the microscopic origin of its reported charge-angular-momentum conversion remains unsettled. Recent theoretical and experimental advances have highlighted a potentially dominant role of orbital transport, raising a fundamental ambiguity between spin- and orbital-mediated conversion in RuO2. Here, we report the first experimental disentanglement of the spin- and orbital-to-charge conversion channels in RuO2 heterostructures using terahertz emission spectroscopy. We identify Fe as a predominantly spin-current injector, whereas Ni and permalloy predominantly inject orbital currents, revealing a substantial orbital contribution to ultrafast terahertz emission. Under controlled spin-current injection, we find no evidence for inverse altermagnetic spin-splitting effect. Instead, the observed anisotropy is consistent with an anisotropic inverse spin Hall response that is strongly conditioned by the near-interface environment. Under orbital-current injection, the anisotropy is markedly weaker, indicating that orbital-to-charge conversion is largely isotropic in RuO2. Our results establish orbital transport and interface-conditioned spin Hall conversion as key to terahertz emission from RuO2, underscoring the need to disentangle spin, orbital, and interfacial contributions before assigning anisotropy to altermagnetism.

title: Momentum-space engineering in van der Waals heterostructures
summary: Twenty years of graphene research have established Dirac fermions as a versatile platform for exploring quantum topological phenomena. Yet control over graphene's low-energy spectrum mostly follows the route of miniband engineering using real-space superlattices. Here we introduce a complementary approach based on momentum-space 'Umklapp' band engineering. This is realised by matching reciprocal space positions of band edges of two adjacent highly incommensurate 2D crystals to coincide upon a boost from their Bragg vectors, creating resonant interlayer hybridisation that qualitatively reconstructs their spectra. To demonstrate this approach experimentally, we use monolayer graphene on MoS$_2$, twisted such that MoS$_2$ Q-valley states are brought by Umklapp into energy-momentum resonance with graphene's Dirac cones. The ensuing hybridization results in the formation of a clear additional Dirac-like spectral feature, identified by a distinct Landau-level fan and Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations characteristic to Berry phase $π$ electrons. These new topological spectral features create a spin-valley locked Ising system which is robust against small twist-angle variations that can be further tuned by an external displacement field. More broadly, Umklapp band engineering offers a practical strategy for tailoring the electronic structure in van der Waals heterostructures, expanding the design space of quantum materials beyond moiré superlattices and weak proximity effects.

title: Helical magnetism from sliding Luttinger liquids in hole-doped twisted bilayer WTe$_2$
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for publication in JPS Conference Proceedings (SCES2026)
summary: We investigate carrier-mediated helical magnetism in hole-doped twisted bilayer WTe$_2$ coupled to localized moments. The itinerant carriers are described by a valleyless two-flavor sliding Luttinger liquid. Via the feedback mechanism of the helical order formed within individual channels, we show that the interchannel spin susceptibility mediates a Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida interaction between localized moments that can stabilize a coherent helical magnetic texture across the coupled-wire array. A spin-wave analysis of the ordered state allows us to estimate the magnon energies and helix-ordering scale. The magnon energies depend on the carrier interactions with representative values falling in the microwave regime, suggesting possible detection by magnetic-resonance techniques. The helical order partially gaps the carrier spectrum and renormalizes the spin-correlation and relaxation exponents. These results identify twisted bilayer WTe$_2$ as a tunable low-dimensional platform for realizing and probing carrier-mediated helical magnetism.

title: Quantum Interference Control of Coupled Atomic Spins
summary: We propose a protocol for the non-resonant electric control of quantum states in atomic-scale spin systems using Landau-Zener-Stückelberg-Majorana (LZSM) interferometry. We focus on a Ti-Ti-Fe trimer on a thin MgO layer, a platform that has recently emerged as a promising candidate for qubit realization using electron spin resonance combined with scanning tunneling microscopy (ESR-STM). We first analyze a Ti dimer in the absence of the Fe atom and show, through a detailed spectroscopic study, that avoided level crossings can be engineered by combining the in-plane component of the external magnetic field, the tip magnetic field, and the applied bias voltage, which allows the system to be tuned electrically through these crossings. Based on this, we develop LZSM protocols for coherent state control in the dimer using non-resonant LZSM-STM. We then consider the full trimer, where the Fe atom generates a local magnetic field at the remote Ti atom, enabling non-local spin control. We show that this remote and non-resonant manipulation reduces unwanted effects associated with tunneling electrons and enables quantum operations on short timescales. Our results show that quantum interference can be used as a resource for electrically driven, non-resonant, and non-local spin control in atomic-scale systems. This approach enables fast quantum operations while mitigating decoherence, offering a promising route toward scalable atom-based qubit architectures.

title: Scanning Probe Control, Quantum Dynamics, and Dispersive Readout of Suspended Carbon Nanotube Resonators
summary: Suspended carbon nanotubes (CNTs) offer promising opportunities for quantum nanomechanics owing to their small effective mass, strong electrostatic tunability, and mechanical nonlinearity. We develop a unified theoretical framework for coherent control and readout of a suspended CNT driven by an atomic force microscope (AFM) tip and capacitively coupled to a Cooper-pair box (CPB). We first derive the linear and nonlinear Duffing response of the CNT and quantify the effects of AFM force gradients, tip-position fluctuations, and voltage noise on mechanical stability, dephasing, and heating. These results establish operating conditions for coherent actuation with limited backaction. We then quantize the Duffing oscillator, derive its Kerr anharmonicity, and identify the requirements for selective control of individual vibrational transitions. Estimates of thermal occupation and active cooling illustrate the constraints for CNT modes spanning frequencies from 54 MHz to 5.37 GHz. Finally, we derive the CNT--CPB interaction and its dispersive limit, showing how phonon number and parity can be mapped onto the CPB through Ramsey interferometry and detected using quantum-capacitance readout. The resulting framework identifies the conditions under which localized AFM actuation, nonlinear quantum dynamics, and superconducting state-resolved detection can operate within a single CNT device.

title: Local Correlations Determine the Dephasing Threshold of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ Topology
summary: In this work, we try to understand the question of how to address the survival of band topology in the presence of dephasing. We investigate this question in the Kane-Mele $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological insulator. To determine the stability of the topological invariant we construct a single particle Hamiltonian that also provides identical correlation at the single particle level. The phase transition from topological to trivial is determined by the gap closing of this correlation Hamiltonian. This gap closing is related to purity gap. As a diagnostics we calculated the invariant directly and as a complementary diagnostic, coherent two-terminal transport through the auxiliary correlation Hamiltonian exhibits quantized conductance in the nontrivial region. This does not establish physical conductance under dephasing. Our results identify a predictive local criterion for the survival of single-particle topological structure under a specified noise channel.

title: Cavity-enhanced second harmonic generation from Rydberg excitons in Cu$_2$O
summary: Rydberg excitons in Cu$_2$O provide a solid-state setting for creating giant optical nonlinearities. Here, we use second-harmonic generation (SHG) to study Rydberg excitons in a doubly resonant optical microcavity designed to enhance both the pump and second-harmonic fields. We observe even-parity exciton states in an optical cavity and extend cavity-based measurements of Rydberg excitons up to $n=10$. The SHG intensity depends strongly on pump cavity detuning, showing the dominant role of the microcavity is the enhancement of the intra-cavity pump field. Analysis reveals an additional enhancement from the resonant second-harmonic cavity giving an overall SHG enhancement factor of $21 \pm 2$ inside the microcavity. These results establish cavity-enhanced SHG spectroscopy as a valuable tool for studying Rydberg excitons in microcavities and provide a pathway towards exploiting optical nonlinearities in Rydberg exciton polariton systems.

title: Exciton design via topological spin textures
summary: Excitons carry energy and information through a semiconductor without carrying charge. This makes them attractive for optoelectronics, but also hard to guide. Magnetic skyrmions, on the other hand, are moved by small electrical currents. Here we develop a theory of excitons interacting with a skyrmion in which the electron and the hole are treated as distinct constituents, each with its own spin--orbit coupling. We find that the topology of the skyrmion is transferred to the exciton only when the exchange coupling exceeds the relevant spin--orbit splitting. The exciton then experiences a full flux quantum, with opposite signs in the two valleys. The quantum metric of the spin texture creates a ring-shaped barrier that traps excitons, whereas the topological charge fixes the angular momentum of the trapped states and hence their optical selection rules. Because the trap moves with the skyrmion, excitons can be transported by current pulses, and small skyrmions accommodate a single exciton, which opens the door for potential hybrid applications in future information technology intertwining topological magnetic bits with optical excitations.

title: Microscopic theory of exciton polarons in transition metal dichalcogenides
summary: Polarons are composite quasiparticles formed when charge carriers strongly couple to lattice vibrations, manifesting as carriers dressed by a surrounding cloud of phonons. Although this dressing fundamentally renormalizes the effective mass and mobility of carriers, its impact on electrically neutral exciton polarons in 2D semiconductors has received limited attention. In particular, despite the growing interest in polaronic effects in atomically thin semiconductors, only a few theoretical studies have addressed spectral signatures and renormalized properties of exciton polarons in these materials. Here, we develop a microscopic model to describe exciton polarons in transition metal dichalcogenides. Applying this model to $1s$ acoustic polarons in an MoSe$_2$ monolayer, we reveal a distinct kink in the polaron dispersion, accompanied by a pronounced broadening of its spectral function. These spectral signatures mark a critical transition from a regime of well-defined bound exciton polarons, characterized by a renormalized energy, reduced group velocity, and enhanced effective mass, to a regime dominated by exciton-phonon scattering. Furthermore, by incorporating intervalley exciton-phonon interaction, we demonstrate that the energetic position of momentum-dark excitons strongly modifies the exciton-polaron lifetime. Overall, our work provides a microscopic framework for determining renormalized properties of exciton polarons and establishes experimentally accessible polaron signatures in 2D semiconductors.

title: Trajectory-Dependent Decoherence and Leakage During Shuttling of Multi-Spin Qubits
comment: 22 pages, 12 figures (including Appendices A--E and the references)
summary: Logical qubits encoded in collective states of multiple spins are promising building blocks for large-scale semiconductor quantum processors. As novel fault-tolerant architectures increasingly rely on qubit shuttling, understanding decoherence of the shuttled multi-spin qubits becomes crucial. We analyze fidelity and leakage of the logical qubits dephased by the spatio-temporally correlated $1/f$ noise, considering two-, three-, and four-spin encodings. We study different shuttling protocols and establish that for all encodings generally, parallel shuttling provides the best protection against decoherence at short distances, whereas sequential shuttling outperforms others for long-range transport (although the exact boundaries depend on the specific device parameters). We explain this common behavior in terms of the dephasing factors of pairs of the shuttled spins; we provide explicit expressions for fidelities and leakage, thus enabling experimentalists to predict performance of the multi-spin qubits from only several independently measured pairwise dephasing factors. Our results establish a connection between shuttling trajectories, noise correlations, and qubit decoherence, and provide guidance for achieving noise-resilient shuttling in scalable semiconductor quantum processors.
